text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Safety warning: a custom CNC router that stalls mid-cycle with no alarm can drop spindle load unexpectedly, lose axis position, or restart motion after a reboot, so lock out spindle power and servo enable before opening the controller cabinet or running any unattended job.
- Most likely root cause is controller cabinet thermal stress from a failing enclosure cooling fan combined with high humidity contamination on the motion-control or PC motherboard side, with 68% confidence.
- The physical mechanism fits the evidence well: a worn fan bearing raises noise, fan RPM falls, cabinet airflow across the CNC controller, motion card, drive logic boards, and power supply heat sinks drops below design cooling, and high ambient humidity adds conductive dust film or light condensation on connectors and PCB surfaces. That combination can cause the industrial PC, Ethernet motion controller, or breakout/control board to hang without generating a clean fault bit, which matches a mid-job stall with no alarm. A reboot temporarily restores operation because the processor, RAM, or motion interface resets after temperature falls for a few minutes.
- No extracted error codes were provided, and none were auto-detected, which actually supports a controller-side freeze more than a servo drive overcurrent or spindle VFD trip, because those faults usually log a code such as following error, overtemp, undervoltage, or drive alarm.
- On custom CNC routers, age and hours matter less than cabinet environment. A noisy fan in a humid shop is a known wear pattern on control enclosures using 80 mm to 120 mm axial fans, DIN-rail power supplies, and PC-based controllers such as Mach3, Mach4, LinuxCNC, Masso, Centroid Acorn, or DSP systems. More data is still required because confidence is below 80%.
- Data Needed
- Cabinet temperature before stall and at stall, measured with an IR thermometer or logged probe in °C at the controller CPU, power supply, and drive heat sink.
- Fan voltage, fan current, and fan RPM or airflow reading, plus clear photos of the fan label, filter media, and cabinet dust pattern.
- Controller platform identification, drive model numbers, power supply output readings in VDC, and any event logs from the CNC software, Windows Event Viewer, Linux syslog, or controller diagnostics page.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Second-ranked cause is intermittent low-voltage DC control power or AC mains sag affecting the controller or motion interface, at 22% likelihood. The mechanism would be a weak 24 VDC supply, loose terminal, oxidized IEC inlet, failing UPS, or line sag under spindle or vacuum load. That can freeze I/O, drop communication, or brown out the controller without a formal alarm. It stays below the primary because the noisy fan and humidity point more directly to thermal/environmental instability than pure power quality.
- Third-ranked cause is intermittent motion-controller communication loss or axis drive enable dropout from corroded connectors, USB/Ethernet instability, or a failing breakout board, at 10% likelihood. The mechanism would be oxidation on RJ45, USB, DB25, or terminal-strip contacts causing packet loss or enable-chain interruption. That can stop motion mid-job and recover after reboot. It ranks below the first two because the fan symptom is a stronger physical clue than a generic comms issue.
- A true servo or stepper drive fault is less likely because most Delta, Leadshine, Yaskawa, Teknic, and similar drives display a local alarm code or LED state when they trip. The absence of any reported drive code, plus the reboot recovery, points upstream toward controller stability.
- A spindle VFD trip is also lower probability because Huanyang, Delta, Hitachi, and similar VFDs usually retain fault codes such as OC, OH, or UV. No such code was reported.
- Custom CNC routers do not have one universal failure pattern, but cabinet cooling failure, contaminated low-voltage electronics, and unstable PC-based control hardware are common across retrofit and small-production machines discussed in Centroid, LinuxCNC, Machsupport, and CNCzone service threads.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Test 1 must be cabinet thermal profiling during a real cutting cycle. Use a 2-channel temperature logger or IR thermometer and record controller CPU area, 24 VDC supply heat sink, and drive heat sink every 5 minutes in °C. If the stall occurs as cabinet temperatures climb above roughly 45 to 55 °C at the controller area, and operation normalizes after cooldown, that confirms the primary thermal hypothesis. If temperatures stay stable below 40 °C, look harder at power or comms. Typical shop cost is $75 to $150.
- Test 2 must be fan performance verification. Use a multimeter for supply voltage, a clamp meter for current if accessible, and either a tachometer or anemometer for RPM/airflow. A healthy 24 VDC fan should see near-rated voltage within about ±10%, and airflow should be strong across the filter and heat sinks. Low RPM with bearing noise confirms the primary cause. Normal fan speed with low supply voltage points toward the power-supply hypothesis. Typical cost is $40 to $90.
- Test 3 must be DC power quality logging on the controller supply rails. Use a DMM plus oscilloscope or data logger on 24 VDC and any 5 VDC/12 VDC rails during spindle start, vacuum start, and axis acceleration. A drop below about 22.8 VDC on a nominal 24 V rail, or ripple above roughly 200 mV on logic rails, supports the secondary power hypothesis. Stable rails during the stall support the primary thermal or tertiary comms cause. Typical cost is $120 to $250.
- Test 4 must be event-log capture from the CNC platform. Pull Windows Event Viewer critical events, Linux dmesg/syslog, controller diagnostics, and drive alarm history. A software hang, USB disconnect, Ethernet timeout, or watchdog reset points toward controller overheating or comms instability. A clean drive undervoltage or axis fault points away from the primary. Typical cost is $60 to $140.
- Test 5 must be connector and contamination inspection under light magnification. Inspect fan filter, PCB surfaces, terminal strips, RJ45/USB connectors, and grounding points for dust film, corrosion, or moisture marks. Visible contamination strongly supports the humidity-assisted primary or tertiary cause. Typical cost is $50 to $120.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- Ask: “What cabinet temperatures in °C did you record at the controller board, power supply, and drive heat sink during a loaded cut?” They should show actual logged numbers or photos. Red flag: “We just felt it and it seemed warm.”
- Ask: “What voltage and RPM or airflow did the enclosure fan measure against its nameplate rating?” They should provide fan label data, measured VDC, and either tach or airflow evidence. Red flag: “The fan spins, so it’s fine.”
- Ask: “What was the minimum 24 VDC and any 5 VDC logic rail reading during spindle and vacuum startup?” They should show meter or scope captures. Red flag: “Power supply tested good on the bench” with no loaded readings.
- Ask: “Can you print or screenshot the controller event log, Windows Event Viewer, Linux log, or drive alarm history from the stall window?” They should produce timestamps and fault history. Red flag: “There were no codes, so there’s nothing to check.”
- Ask: “What contamination or corrosion did you find on filters, connectors, and PCB surfaces, and do you have close-up photos?” They should show cabinet photos before cleaning. Red flag: “We cleaned it already” with no documentation.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: say, “I’ve done some research and want to understand whether the stall is coming from cabinet heat, low-voltage power, or controller communication before any parts are replaced.”
- Phrasing: keep every question tied to a measurement, such as “I’m curious what the 24 VDC rail dropped to during spindle start” instead of “Did you miss a bad power supply?”
- Example dialogue: “I’ve done some research and want to understand what cabinet temperature you measured at the controller when the machine stalled.” “I’ve done some research and want to understand whether the enclosure fan was checked for actual RPM or airflow, not just whether it spins.” “I’ve done some research and want to understand what the minimum 24 VDC reading was under load.” “I’ve done some research and want to understand whether the controller logs show a watchdog reset, USB disconnect, or Ethernet timeout.” “I’ve done some research and want to understand what contamination you found on the board surfaces and connectors.”
- Body language: bring a notebook, ask for photos and readings, and pause after each answer so the technician fills the silence with specifics like 24.1 VDC, 52 °C, or fan model data.
- Response handling: if they get defensive, say, “I’m not questioning your experience; I’m trying to approve the right repair based on measured values.”
- Exit strategy: if they resist giving readings, say, “I’d like to hold off on parts authorization until I have the temperature, voltage, and log data in writing.”
- NEVER say: “My AI report says...” or “I got a second opinion online.”
- ALWAYS say: “I’ve done some research and want to understand...”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Fair primary-cause repair pricing usually starts with an enclosure fan, filter media, cabinet cleaning, connector treatment, and thermal verification. Common fan sizes such as 80 mm, 92 mm, or 120 mm AC or 24 VDC cabinet fans typically cost $15 to $90 each depending on brand, with filter assemblies at $10 to $40.
- If the cabinet uses an industrial panel fan/filter unit from Rittal, Hoffman, Pfannenberg, or similar, a complete replacement assembly can run $90 to $280. If the controller PC fan or CPU cooler is also failing, add $20 to $120 for cooling hardware.
- Labor for access, lockout, cleaning, fan replacement, connector reseating, and loaded retest is typically 1.5 to 3.5 hours at $95 to $165 per hour, or about $145 to $575 labor.
- If contamination is heavy and the shop performs board-safe cleaning with ESD handling, add 0.5 to 1.5 hours, or $50 to $250.
- A fair total for the primary repair path is usually $220 to $850 if no controller board is damaged. If the shop jumps straight to a motion card, industrial PC, or full control retrofit without temperature and voltage data, that is not justified by the current evidence.
- No shop quote was provided, so the main overcharge marker is replacing a controller, VFD, or all axis drives before proving fan failure, thermal rise, or power instability.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts-cannon behavior on this symptom usually means replacing the spindle VFD, one or more stepper/servo drives, limit switches, or the entire breakout board before anyone logs cabinet temperature or 24 VDC under load.
- Another shortcut is declaring “software glitch” and reinstalling Mach3, Mach4, LinuxCNC, or the controller package without checking fan airflow, filter blockage, or Windows Event Viewer disconnect events.
- Price gouging red flags include charging 4 to 6 labor hours for a simple fan and filter replacement, billing premium markup on commodity fans above about 2.5x street price, or recommending a $1,500 to $5,000 control retrofit with no oscilloscope captures, no thermal data, and no contamination photos.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: paid diagnostic time for thermal logging, loaded 24 VDC testing, event-log capture, and cabinet inspection with photos. Those tests directly separate the three ranked causes.
- Approve immediately: replacement of an obviously noisy enclosure fan and clogged filter if the shop documents the fan model, measured voltage, and before/after airflow or temperature improvement.
- Reject outright: replacement of spindle VFD, all axis drives, or the entire controller stack without measured evidence such as undervoltage, drive alarm history, or controller watchdog resets.
- Get a second opinion if the shop cannot identify the controller platform, cannot produce voltage readings in VDC, or says “no codes means no problem” on a CNC system that clearly stalls mid-job.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- A custom CNC router usually depends on three layers working together: the motion controller or industrial PC generates axis commands, the low-voltage power supply keeps logic stable at 24 VDC and often 5 VDC, and the axis drives execute motion while the spindle VFD handles spindle speed.
- The reason a bad cabinet fan matters is that control electronics are temperature-sensitive long before they visibly fail. As fan bearings wear, noise rises and airflow falls. Heat then builds around the CPU, RAM, motion card, Ethernet switch, or breakout board. At the same time, high humidity can leave a thin conductive film on PCB surfaces and connectors, especially where dust collects near fan inlets and terminal strips.
- That heat-plus-humidity combination can create timing errors, communication dropouts, or processor hangs. Because the controller may freeze before it can write a formal fault, the machine can simply stop moving with no alarm. A reboot clears volatile faults, reinitializes USB or Ethernet links, and temporarily restores operation until temperature and contamination conditions return.
- By contrast, a true drive fault usually leaves a code on the drive display, and a true spindle VFD fault usually leaves an overcurrent, overheat, or undervoltage code. That distinction is why temperature logging and power logging are more valuable here than random parts replacement.
- Prevention for this exact failure mode is practical: replace noisy fans before airflow collapses, change filter media on a schedule tied to dust load, keep cabinet doors sealed, maintain a small anti-condensation heater if the shop sees dew-point swings, and inspect 24 VDC terminals annually for oxidation and torque.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Because the machine is custom, the best “OEM” strategy is to match the installed controller and enclosure hardware by exact part number from the fan label, power-supply label, and controller model plate. Good fan brands include ebm-papst, Orion, Sunon, NMB, and Delta; good DIN power supplies include Mean Well, PULS, Phoenix Contact, and Siemens.
- For a cabinet cooling repair, OEM branding is less critical than matching voltage, airflow in CFM or m³/h, bearing type, temperature rating, and filter-frame dimensions. A cheap sleeve-bearing fan in a humid cabinet is a false economy.
- For the controller, motion card, or industrial PC, OEM or exact-compatible parts matter much more because firmware, plugin support, and I/O pin mapping can break with substitutes. A Centroid Acorn, Masso, Ethernet SmoothStepper, or proprietary DSP controller should be replaced only after confirming the exact model and software revision.
- Pricing sources worth checking include Digi-Key, Mouser, Newark, Galco, and manufacturer distributors for fans and power supplies, plus the controller maker’s own parts channel for motion hardware.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Anchor the discussion to the diagnostic sequence, not to the shop’s intuition. Say, “Before I approve anything beyond $250 to $400 of diagnostics, I need the cabinet temperature log, fan readings, and loaded 24 VDC readings.”
- If they quote a fan, filter, and cleaning repair above the fair $220 to $850 range, ask them to separate parts from labor and justify each labor step in hours. A reasonable line item is 1.5 to 3.5 hours, not an open-ended estimate.
- If they recommend a controller or motion card, ask, “What event-log entry, watchdog reset, or communication fault proves the board is bad rather than overheated or undervoltage?” That forces evidence.
- Your walk-away point is any estimate that includes major electronics replacement without measured VDC sag, thermal rise, or logged communication faults. Your leverage is that a custom CNC retrofit can become expensive quickly, so disciplined diagnostics protect both sides from unnecessary parts.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: controller cabinet overheating from a failing cooling fan plus humidity contamination, 68% confidence. The noisy fan is the strongest physical clue, and the no-alarm stall with reboot recovery matches a controller or motion-interface hang more than a drive trip.
- Secondary cause: intermittent low-voltage control power or AC mains sag, 22% confidence. This can also create no-code freezes or resets, especially when spindle and dust collection loads hit the same branch, but the fan symptom keeps it ranked lower.
- Tertiary cause: intermittent controller communication loss or enable-chain dropout from corroded connectors or failing interface hardware, 10% confidence. High humidity supports connector oxidation, but there is not enough evidence yet to rank it above thermal or power causes.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediately stop unattended production runs until the cabinet fan, filter, and control power rails are tested under load, because a mid-job stall can scrap material, break cutters, or create an unsafe restart condition.
- Replace any noisy enclosure fan now if the model and voltage are confirmed, then clean or replace filter media and document before/after cabinet temperatures during a loaded cut. That is a low-cost, high-yield first repair on this symptom set.
- Add a maintenance interval based on shop dust and humidity: inspect fan noise monthly, inspect filter restriction monthly, verify cabinet seal condition quarterly, and log 24 VDC output annually under load. In humid environments, consider a small anti-condensation heater or dehumidified control enclosure if morning condensation is present.
- Monitor for warning signs such as longer reboot recovery, random USB/Ethernet disconnects, warm controller housings above about 50 °C, dim HMI behavior, or fan noise changes. Those signs point to the same failure chain before a full no-start occurs.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Schneider Electric technical guidance on enclosure thermal management and fan/filter sizing directly supports the overheating mechanism in control cabinets: https://www.se.com/ww/en/work/support/resources-and-tools/thermal-management/
- PULS application guidance on 24 VDC power supply behavior, voltage sag, and diagnostics is directly relevant to the secondary low-voltage hypothesis: https://www.pulspower.com/us/support/application-notes/
- LinuxCNC documentation and forum resources on motion-controller communication faults, watchdog behavior, and log review are directly relevant if this router uses a PC-based controller: https://linuxcnc.org/docs/ and https://forum.linuxcnc.org/
- Machsupport forum archives on Mach3/Mach4 USB/Ethernet motion freezes and controller communication issues are directly relevant if the machine uses a Mach-based control stack: https://www.machsupport.com/forum/
- CNCzone service discussions on cabinet cooling, dust contamination, and intermittent control freezes provide independent field confirmation across custom router builds: https://www.cnczone.com/forums/

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Authorize only three diagnostics first: cabinet temperature logging during a loaded cut, fan voltage/RPM or airflow testing, and loaded 24 VDC rail logging with event-log capture.
- Replace the noisy enclosure fan and clogged filter media immediately if the shop documents the exact fan rating and before/after airflow or temperature improvement.
- Decline any quote for VFD, axis drives, or full controller replacement until the shop provides actual °C, VDC, and log evidence that rules out thermal and power causes.
